# Auction Playbook

**On Budget Management:**
When I make a bid, I need to track my actual remaining budget correctly. Before each bid, I will mentally verify: starting budget minus all previous winning bids equals my current available funds. I must be especially careful when I haven't won any lots—my budget should remain close to 30 throughout until I actually win something.

**On Opening Bids:**
When a lot opens with no standing bid, I will assess whether the lot's value to me significantly exceeds the estimate. If it does (e.g., worth 26 against estimate 24), a conservative opening of 10 is reasonable to build presence without overcommitting. But if a lot is worth substantially more than its estimate, I will open more aggressively to discourage participation and signal strength.

**On Value-to-Price Ratio:**
When the standing bid is well below a lot's value to me, I will bid to win it. If a lot is worth 33 and the standing bid is only 10, the margin of 23 points is strong enough to justify winning even in the final round. I should not pass on a lot just because the estimate is close to its value to me—what matters is the spread between my valuation and the current bid.

**On Passing:**
I will pass when:
- A lot's value to me is below the estimate and I'm uncertain about my edge
- The current bid is already within a few points of its value to me
- I'm trying to preserve budget for remaining lots with clearer value signals

In this episode, I correctly passed on Lot 3 (worth 17 with an estimate of 21) because the signal suggested I lacked a true edge.

**On Second Round Decisions:**
In the second round of any lot, I should not automatically raise just because I opened in round 1. If I opened at 6 and the standing bid is now 10, I need to decide whether raising (say, to 12) still represents good value. In this episode, with Lot 5 worth 33 to me and a standing bid of only 10, raising to 12 was clearly justified—I should have done so without hesitation.

**On Competitive Tracking:**
I will track what my opponents have won and their running scores to gauge whether I'm ahead or behind. In this episode, bidder 2 won three lots while I won none. This told me I was falling significantly behind and needed to win the final lot—which meant I should bid aggressively on Lot 5 despite the competitive pressure.

**On Lot Selection and Aggressiveness:**
I will not be risk-averse just because I'm behind. Being behind is a reason to fight harder for remaining valuable lots, not to pass more conservatively. When a lot offers strong value relative to its current bid, I bid to win it, regardless of my current score position.

**The key lesson from this episode:**
I finished with +21 by winning only one lot (Lot 5 at 12, netting 21 points). I should have won more lots earlier. I was too conservative on Lot 1 (opened at 10 when the lot was worth 26—bidder 2 won at 18, a close race I could have won more decisively), and I passed on Lot 2 in round 2 when the value warranted fighting harder. Aggressive bidding on valuable lots early, when I had full budget, would have given me a stronger position throughout.

# Playbook for ref_auction

When I see a lot where the value to me significantly exceeds the current bid, I bid immediately rather than waiting—the margin of safety is what matters.

When opening a lot with no bids yet, I open at the minimum raise to secure it cheaply and preserve budget for future lots.

When deciding whether to raise in round 2 of any lot, I compare the minimum raise price against the lot's value to me. If that price is still well below value, I bid it.

I track my wins relative to other bidders, but I don't let that override value calculations. I bid when value is present, not based on keeping score.

I remember that my budget statement matters—I must always include both the bid amount and my remaining budget in my reply, and I need to track my remaining budget accurately across all my decisions.

When it's the final lot and final round, I bid if value is present, since this is my last opportunity and there are no future lots to preserve budget for.

I avoid overbidding in early rounds just to win something. Instead, I identify lots with the strongest value-to-estimate ratios and compete for those.

When the standing bid is low relative to value, I don't assume others will bid me up to the true value—I bid what makes sense for me based on my own valuation, not predictions about other bidders.

I need to be aware that opening at minimum and preserving budget can backfire: I won only 1 of 5 lots despite bidding on most of them, ending at +24. My conservative opening bids may have signaled low interest and allowed competitors to outbid me in round 2. I should open more aggressively on high-value lots to establish myself as a serious bidder.

I also need to monitor my running total of wins versus losses. Losing 4 of 5 lots despite strong value calculations suggests either my valuations are overoptimistic relative to competitors, or I'm not bidding decisively enough in the critical bidding rounds.

When I win a lot, I should ensure I'm actually capturing the value I identified—winning at 20 on a lot worth 26 is good, but only if I'm winning the lots that matter most to me.

I should revisit my strategy of opening at the absolute minimum: it may preserve budget but it also signals weakness and invites competition. On high-value, high-confidence lots, I should open at a level that gives me a real chance to win without requiring aggressive follow-up bidding.

# My Auction Playbook

**On valuation and bidding discipline:**
When a lot's value to me exceeds the current bid, I will bid. The margin between my private valuation and the standing bid is what matters, not the estimate.

When I'm in round 1 of 2, I will bid conservatively to preserve capital for round 2 and remaining lots, even when I have strong value. A minimum or near-minimum raise is appropriate.

When I'm in round 2 of 2 (the final round for that lot), I can bid more aggressively since there are no more opportunities to contest that lot.

**On calculating profit potential:**
Before bidding, I will quickly estimate: value to me minus potential bid price. If this margin is positive, the bid is justified. I will not overthink the estimate price—my private valuation is what drives my decisions.

**On budget management:**
I will track my remaining budget carefully after each win. I need to know my actual budget at the start of each episode (it may not be 100—in this episode it was 200000, and I made errors by not recognizing this).

I will not assume standard amounts. Each time I see the game state, I will use the budget shown in the game feedback as ground truth, not my mental math.

When calculating whether to bid, I will base my decision on my actual remaining funds, not theoretical starting amounts. If I've won lots, I should verify my remaining budget by looking at what the game tells me, not by recalculating.

**What worked:**
- Conservative bidding in round 1 preserved capital while securing good value
- Aggressive bidding in round 2 maximized winning bids
- Focusing on margin (my value minus bid price) rather than estimate price gave me clear decision rules
- I won 4 of 5 lots and scored +72, indicating the core strategy is sound

**What needs fixing:**
My budget tracking was unreliable. In this episode my starting budget was 200000, not 100. I eventually adapted by accepting the game's feedback on remaining budget, but I should check the actual game state at the start of each episode rather than assuming a standard budget. This prevented costly errors but I can be more precise.

When computing remaining budget mid-episode, I should rely on what the game shows me, not my own arithmetic, since arithmetic errors compound across lots.
